Internment is the act of officially confining or imprisoning a person — or more often, an entire group of people — without charging them with a specific crime and without giving them a proper trial.

It is something a government or authority does to people it considers a danger or a threat, typically during a war, a political crisis, or a national emergency. The people being held have not necessarily done anything wrong. They are confined simply because of who they are — their nationality, their ethnicity, their religion, or their political beliefs.
What Makes Internment Different from Ordinary Imprisonment

This is the most important distinction to understand.

When someone is imprisoned in the normal legal sense, there is a process: they are accused of a specific crime, they go to court, evidence is presented, and a judge or jury decides whether they are guilty. Only then are they locked up.

Internment skips all of that. There is no charge. There is no trial. There is no verdict. The authority simply decides — often by government order — that a certain group of people is a risk, and rounds them up. This is why internment is considered by many to be a deeply unjust practice, even when the government doing it argues it is "necessary" for safety or security.

It is collective, not individual. Ordinary imprisonment targets a specific person for a specific act. Internment targets people as a group, based on a shared characteristic. If you belong to that group, you can be interned — regardless of whether you personally have done anything wrong.

It is authorised by the state. Internment is not kidnapping or an illegal act carried out in secret. It is an official, government-sanctioned policy. This is what separates it from other forms of unlawful detention.

It is indefinite. Internment does not come with a fixed sentence. Interned people are typically held for as long as the authority decides it is necessary — which in practice can mean months or years.

It usually happens during emergencies. Governments most commonly justify internment by pointing to a war, a security threat, or a state of emergency. The argument is usually that the normal pace of law is too slow, and that holding these people is necessary to protect the public.

The clearest and most famous example is the internment of Japanese Americans during World War II. After Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in 1941, the United States government, fearing that Japanese Americans might be loyal to Japan, forcibly relocated around 120,000 people of Japanese descent — most of whom were American citizens — into internment camps. They lost their homes, their businesses, and their freedom, not because of anything they had done, but purely because of their ancestry. The US government later formally acknowledged this as a grave injustice.

Similarly, the British government interned hundreds of people in Northern Ireland in the 1970s during the height of the conflict known as "The Troubles." Suspected members and supporters of the IRA were held without trial. This policy was deeply controversial and is widely regarded as having worsened the conflict rather than helped it.

During both World Wars, many countries also interned civilians who were nationals of enemy countries — for example, German or Austro-Hungarian immigrants living in Britain or the United States were sometimes interned simply because of their national origin.

There is also a legally recognised and more neutral form of internment: the internment of prisoners of war (POWs). Under international law (specifically the Geneva Conventions), soldiers captured during a war can be lawfully held by the opposing side until the conflict ends. This is also called internment, though it is treated separately from civilian internment and comes with specific protections.

A person who is interned is called an internee. The facility where internees are held is called an internment camp. These camps vary enormously — from basic, fenced enclosures to more elaborate facilities — but the defining feature is always the same: people are held there against their will, without trial.
The Moral and Legal Weight of the Word

It is important to understand that internment carries a heavy negative connotation in modern usage. While governments have historically defended it as a wartime necessity, it is now widely seen as a violation of fundamental human rights — specifically the right to liberty and the right to a fair trial. Many international human rights frameworks and legal scholars consider mass civilian internment, particularly when based on ethnicity or religion, to be a form of persecution.

When you hear or read the word "internment" today, it almost always appears in a context where someone is being critical of a government's actions, examining a historical injustice, or debating the limits of state power.

To see how the word is used naturally:

  • "The internment of Japanese Americans during World War II remains one of the darkest chapters in US history."
  • "Human rights organisations condemned the government's policy of internment without trial."
  • "Survivors of the internment spoke about the years they lost, imprisoned for no crime."

In short, internment is the official, government-ordered confinement of people — usually a group — without trial or charge, most often during a war or crisis. It differs from ordinary imprisonment because it requires no proof of wrongdoing and targets people based on who they are, not what they have done. It is a word that sits at the intersection of law, politics, and human rights, and it almost always signals a serious — and often condemned — exercise of state power over individuals.
